Valuation vs own history (VL3) uses trailing P/E: free forward P/E history is too short.

VL3's 5-year P/E median (87.3x) is overstated: the collector derives fourth-quarter EPS as full year minus three quarters, which goes wrong across stock splits (Q4 FY Jan 2022 shows −$1.09 instead of $1.18; Q4 FY Jan 2025 −$4.49 instead of $0.89). A $400m provision on excess H200 inventory (10-Q, first half of FY27) is not removed from DM6 because its split between quarters is not disclosed; removing it would raise the latest margin by about 0.1 point.
Trailing GAAP earnings include $23.7bn of first-half gains on equity holdings, so the trailing P/E (30.0x) understates the operating P/E (about 34x without them).

DM4a, DM4b and DM5 are entered by hand at each results date (Nvidia CFO commentary; cloud companies' reports). DM5 mixes bases: Alphabet reports cash capex only, the others include finance leases; Microsoft's change to data-centre asset lives will distort future comparisons.

One driver: price trend, Demand and Valuation all depend on the AI capex cycle and the FY28 consensus ($15.91); the driver cap does not bite when every input is bullish, so 'High' confidence overstates how much independent evidence there is.

Not scored: customers' own chips (Google TPU, Amazon Trainium), power and grid delays to data-centre build-outs, memory prices (HBM reported up to +50% in 2027), and a low P/E on possibly peak earnings. segments.name: Data Center
segments.sells: AI accelerators (GPUs and full rack systems such as Blackwell and Vera Rubin), the CPUs and networking that link them, and software.
segments.buyers: The big clouds (Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Oracle: 'Hyperscale', about 55% of Data Center in the July quarter) and AI clouds, AI labs, sovereign and corporate buyers ('ACIE', about 45%).
pos: Grew 117% in the July quarter vs a year earlier; the fastest-growing part.
Sold as complete systems with networking and software, which makes customers stickier and supports a 75% company gross margin.
Demand is broadening: ACIE grew 138% vs a year earlier.
neg: Not contracted recurring revenue: it depends on customers' capex budgets, which are cyclical.
A handful of direct customers buy most of it (one was 16% of company revenue in the July quarter).
Several of the biggest buyers design their own chips (Google TPU, Amazon Trainium) with Broadcom and Marvell.
China Data Center sales are near zero (under 1% of Data Center revenue in the July quarter); China in total was about 13% of company revenue in the year to Jan 2025.
Part of the demand is financed by Nvidia itself: guarantees of up to $105bn on a data-centre campus leased to OpenAI, and $47.9bn of stakes in unlisted companies, many of them AI customers.

segments.name: Edge Computing (gaming, workstations, auto, other)
segments.sells: Gaming GPUs, professional workstations, chips for cars and robots, PCs and AI-RAN telecom equipment.
segments.buyers: Gamers and PC makers, designers and engineers, carmakers and robot builders, telecom operators.
pos: Grew 27% in the July quarter vs a year earlier.
Spreads Nvidia's platform into PCs, cars and robots, a longer-dated growth option.
neg: Small: under a tenth of revenue.
Consumer PC sales slowed as memory made PCs dearer (Nvidia, Q2 FY27).
Concentration: Data Center is 92% of sales (last 4 quarters).

shift.title: What the shift means for Nvidia
pos: Data Center rose from 67% of sales to 92% in 3 years (last 4 quarters vs the 4 quarters to Jul 2023), and company gross margin rose from 64.6% to 74.7% over the same period: the AI systems business carries the margin.
Data Center sales grew 90% over the last 4 quarters vs the 4 quarters before; Edge Computing grew 35%.
Free cash flow (operating cash minus capital spending) was $127.0bn over the last 12 months to Jul 2026.
neg: Concentration has risen: over nine-tenths of sales now depend on data-centre capex budgets that can be cut quickly.
The biggest buyers are also building alternatives (Google TPU, Amazon Trainium), so share of their spend is not guaranteed.
Margin is guided down 1 point for the October quarter (74.0% vs 75.0%) on memory costs.

bubble.history: Back-checked on monthly data 1998-2026: Breaking first fired in Aug 2000, Oct 2007 and Mar 2022, each within 0-5 months of the market top and before most of the fall (S&P 500 then fell a further 40%, 53% and 21%). False alarms: Aug 2011, Nov 2018 and Mar 2023, after which the S&P 500 was 14-28% higher a year later. It confirms a top is probably in; it does not call it in advance.
